arguments.conclusion: Historical data from 1960-1980 shows that raising the Fed funds rate preceded rising inflation (the opposite of conventional theory), and since 2000 the simple correlation has broken down, indicating that other factors dominate and the conventional rate-inflation relationship is inverted or unreliable.

arguments.premise_synthesis: From 1960 to 1980, interest rates and inflation moved in lock step: when the Fed raised rates in 1961, inflation rose in 1962; when rates were lowered in 1969, inflation fell; when rates rose in 1972, inflation rose; and when rates were lowered in 1974, inflation fell—contradicting the conventional view that higher rates reduce inflation. Since 2000, the simple correlation has broken down: from 2002–2004 the Fed lowered rates yet inflation rose; 2004–2006 rates rose and inflation eventually fell; 2007 rates fell and inflation rose; and after 2020, rates were lowered to zero, inflation spiked, then rates were raised and inflation fell. These later episodes indicate that other factors (such as debt and money supply) now dominate the relationship, but the overall pattern still refutes the textbook claim that higher rates reliably reduce inflation.
arguments.conclusion_supported: The Fed funds rate and inflation have shown a historically inverted relationship (1960–1980) and a more complex but still non-conventional relationship since 2000, undermining the standard monetary policy framework that assumes raising rates will reduce inflation.
